title: Slightly Weaker, But Much Stronger on The Week
summary:
Slightly Weaker, But Much Stronger on The Week 

             
             
            Friday was calm and sideways in the bigger picture. Sure, a 4+ bp increase in 10yr yields and an MBS decline of just over an eighth of a point might sound somewhat unpleasant on the average day, but considering we saw 4 times as much movement in the other, friendlier direction yesterday, we're not bothered. Rationale was rational to boot. The NASDAQ drifted sideways to slightly higher and nittier grittier canaries like Coreweave bond yields bounced back slightly lower as well. Overall, today did nothing to change the big picture. We're still waiting to see if tech sentiment gets back on track or continues to deteriorate. It won't be able to equivocate for long.

title: Modest Uptick in Rates But Still Near 1-Month Lows
summary: Yesterday was an exciting day for rates with the lowest levels since September 23rd and a fairly brisk decline versus the previous day.   Today? Fairly boring by comparison. Rates were technically a hair higher, which isn't too surprising given the prevailing motivations in the tech sector. Yesterday's rate rally coincided with heavy selling in tech stocks. With those same stocks avoiding drama today (and the NASDAQ moving slightly higher overall), bond yields (aka "rates") also inched higher.  The average mortgage lender moved up 0.03% for a top-tier 30yr fixed scenario leaving our index at 7.33%. This matches October 15th's levels in a tie for the 2nd lowest since September 23rd.   [thirtyyearmortgagerates]

title: Mortgage Applications Aren't Ready to Rebound Just Yet
summary:
Mortgage applications continued to decline even as mortgage rates finally moved lower. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported a  5.3% drop  in total application volume for the week ending October 16, despite the first weekly decline in mortgage rates in more than two months.  The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate fell to  7.41%  from 7.50% the previous week. That improvement wasn't enough to revive demand, with both purchase and refinance applications moving lower.  The seasonally adjusted Purchase Index fell  7%  for the week and was  18% below year-ago levels . Refinances fared somewhat better, declining 2%, though activity remained  59% lower  than a year earlier.  “Purchase applications fell 18 percent behind last year's pace, as higher rates are pricing buyers out of the market,” said MBA's Joel Kan, who also noted that adjustable-rate mortgages remain an option for qualified borrowers looking for lower rates. ARMs held steady at  10.5% of applications , with rates nearly a full percentage point below the 30-year fixed average.  The refinance share of total applications increased to  39.0%  from 37.7% the previous week. That shift came despite the decline in refinance volume, reflecting the steeper drop in purchase applications.   Mortgage Rate Summary:

title: Building Permits Hold Steady Despite Slide in Housing Starts
summary: Residential construction failed to find even footing in September, with housing starts declining and single-family building permits pulling back, while total permits held nearly steady and completions edged higher. This week's Census Bureau data highlights weakness in new construction, particularly on the single-family side, while starts and completions were comparatively stable.    Privately owned housing starts fell  5.2%  to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of  1.221 million , down  7.4%  from September 2025. Single-family starts declined  4.6%  to  859k , and multi-family came in at  349k .  Building permits were more stable, slipping just  0.2%  to an annual rate of  1.400 million , although they were  3.0%  below the September 2025 pace. Single-family authorizations fell  4.0%  to  845k , while multi-family permits rose to  503k .  The contrast between total permits and single-family authorizations suggests that the overall pipeline for future construction was relatively steady, even as the single-family segment weakened. Multi-family permits accounted for a larger share of total authorizations in September, though monthly figures can fluctuate considerably in that segment.    Housing completions bounced back from last month, and increased  2.2%  to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of  1.192 million , still  14.0%  below the September 2025 rate. Single-family completions slipped  2.4%  to  840k , multi-family completions came in at  339k .

  "Buyer traffic has now fallen to its lowest level since April 2012, excluding the initial pandemic shock in April 2020.” said NAHB Chairman Bill Owens. title: Et Tu, S&P PMI?
summary: Little has changed between yesterday's close and this morning's early trading. 10yr yields are still several bps under 5%. MBS are still effectively at the highest levels in a month.  Tech isn't happy, with futures hugging yesterday's lows ahead of the open. One difference, however, is that we'll get a piece of economic data this morning that had a shockingly big impact on bonds when it came out last month: S&P PMIs. We're still incredulous about the 9/23 sell-off being driven by S&P PMIs, but we haven't seen a better explanation. That said, the jury's out as to whether that's a one-off. It would be very interesting if today's numbers (due out at 9:45 ET) are far from forecast, because whether they're better or worse, we'd definitely be learning something new.

title: Mortgage Rates Edge Down To 7.32%, Offering Limited Pipeline Relief
summary: The first mortgage-rate decline in two months trims about $22 from the monthly payment on a $400,000 loan. For LOs trying to salvage year-end transactions, that creates an opening among borrowers already close to making the numbers work.Freddie Mac reported Thursday that the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate fell to 7.32% from 7.40% the previous week. The average 15-year rate edged down to 6.68% from 6.71%.“The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage declined this week, offering some relief to prospective homebuyers,” said Sam Khater, Freddie Mac’s chief economist.

title: Trump Targets Mortgage Insurance, Refi Costs In Sweeping Housing Order
summary: President Donald Trump signed a sweeping executive order Thursday aimed at lowering the cost of homeownership, targeting everything from mortgage insurance premiums and refinancing fees to appraisal requirements and loan-level price adjustments.For mortgage lenders and originators, some of the most consequential provisions extend beyond the administration's headline promises of cheaper housing. The order directs the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to consider eliminating certain refinancing expenses, easing documentation requirements, and expanding alternatives to traditional title insurance.

title: More Homebuyer Assistance Programs Skip Income Caps, Accept Repeat Buyers
summary: A borrower’s income or previous homeownership may leave more room for purchase assistance than an originator expects. Down Payment Resource identified 311 homeownership programs without income restrictions in the third quarter, up from 291 in the second quarter, while 1,080 programs carried no first-time homebuyer requirement.The findings offer a reason to broaden assistance screening beyond lower-income, first-time buyers. They also come with a practical qualification: the number of programs lenders can put to work immediately grew much more slowly than the overall inventory.

title: Home Affordability Gap Persists Even With 20% Down
summary: A $73,600 down payment still leaves the average worker short of the income needed to afford the nation’s median-priced home under ATTOM’s latest affordability calculation.The national median home sales price fell to $368,000 in the third quarter of 2026, down from $375,000 a year earlier, according to ATTOM’s U.S. Home Affordability Report, released Oct. 22. Wage growth also outpaced home-price growth in a majority of the counties studied.
